analysis.one_liner: Guarantees the right to abortion before viability nationwide and blocks state bans and restrictions.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote or a floor vote in the 118th Congress, despite all 216 House Democrats cosponsoring it.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would bar federal, state, and local governments from banning abortion before fetal viability or restricting abortion procedures, medication abortion, telemedicine, and immediate care when delay threatens health. After viability, states could still restrict abortion except when needed for the patient's life or health. It would also protect the right to travel to another state for care and let the Justice Department, patients, and providers sue officials who enforce bans, overriding state immunity.
analysis.who_benefits: People who can become pregnant, especially the 17.8 million women of reproductive age in the 14 states where the bill's findings say abortion had become unavailable after the Dobbs decision, plus the clinics and providers who would regain legal protection to serve them [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Bars governments from prohibiting abortion before fetal viability or restricting particular procedures, medication abortion, telemedicine, or immediate care when delay poses a health risk.
After viability, governments may still restrict abortion, but not when the provider judges it necessary to protect the patient's life or health.
Protects a right to interstate travel for reproductive health care, including abortion, and a right to help someone else exercise it.

Lets the Attorney General, patients, and providers sue states and officials who enforce banned restrictions, abrogating state and Tenth and Eleventh Amendment immunity, and awards attorney's fees to prevailing plaintiffs.

The bill's findings document that after Dobbs, abortion became unavailable in 14 states, 66 clinics in 15 states stopped offering abortions, and travel time to a clinic more than tripled, imposing lost wages, travel, and child care costs.

analysis.who_pays: State governments and officials who enforce abortion bans and restrictions would face federal lawsuits from the Justice Department, patients, and providers, and would lose the power to keep those laws on the books. Federal courts would absorb the resulting litigation.

drawbacks.text: The bill goes beyond simply blocking bans: it also forbids requirements that apply only to abortion, such as mandatory in-person visits, mandatory disclosure of reasons, medically inaccurate counseling scripts, and facility or staffing rules not imposed on medically comparable procedures [S3]. Opponents who accept the legitimacy of some regulation argue this preempts the whole field of state abortion law rather than only prohibitions.

Section 7 preempts any inconsistent state or federal law, including the Religious Freedom Restoration Act, and Section 9 strips states of sovereign immunity in these suits [S3]. That is an unusually broad override of state law and of a federal religious-liberty statute, which courts would have to sort out for years.

The enforcement mechanism relies on litigation: rights become real only through court cases against state officials, so access in hostile states would be contested clinic-by-clinic, law-by-law, and could be undone if a court limited the bill's constitutional basis.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is concrete and large: restoring legal access to abortion in states that banned it, ending a patchwork where 17.8 million women of reproductive age had no in-state access and travel burdens more than tripled [S3]. The cost is a genuine reduction in state authority over abortion regulation and a broad preemption that reaches regulations short of bans, all of which would be tested through years of litigation. The tradeoff is real, but the bill's central effect is to expand access for ordinary people.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, sent to two House committees, and referred to a health subcommittee, and that is where it sat until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Judy Chu introduced the bill in the House on March 30, 2023, with a large bloc of cosponsors listed at introduction.
The bill was referred to the Committee on Energy and Commerce and to the Committee on the Judiciary, with consideration split between them at the Speaker's discretion.
On April 7, 2023, it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health.
No further action appears in the record: the bill received no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
Every one of the 216 House Democrats cosponsored the bill, while no House Republican did.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: States with abortion bans and their restrictive laws remain in effect because no federal floor was ever enacted. House Republicans were also spared a politically difficult vote, since the bill never reached the floor.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had no roll-call votes in this Congress, but its support map was entirely one-sided: all 216 House Democrats signed on as cosponsors and no House Republican did, and with Republicans holding a 224-seat House majority the bill never advanced past committee referral.

industries.note: Providers regain a statutory right to offer abortion services free of state bans and abortion-specific regulations, and can sue to stop enforcement. The bill's findings report 66 clinics across 15 states closing after Dobbs; this bill is aimed at reopening that channel of care. The bill explicitly does not change how insurance covers abortion, so it does not channel public money through the industry.

The bill protects providers' ability to prescribe and dispense abortion drugs under evidence-based regimens and counts pharmacies among covered providers, removing state limits on medication abortion. No public subsidy is involved.

These governments would face Justice Department and private lawsuits, lose sovereign immunity defenses, and be required to stop enforcing bans and abortion-specific restrictions. Their interest in continuing to restrict access runs directly against the access ordinary patients would gain.
